The post does not publish one full tool-call transcript; it reports observed behavior of **Opus 4.5 on the Claude Agent SDK**, looped across many context windows, on a high-level prompt such as **“build a clone of claude.ai.”** Compaction was already available. Unless noted, this is the **unharnessed / insufficiently prompted** run.

---

### Task and setup

Claude was asked to build a production-quality web app (a claude.ai clone) from a high-level prompt only. Work could not finish in one context window, so the same agent loop was continued across discrete sessions. Each new session started with **no memory of prior sessions**. Compaction was used inside a session but was the only continuity mechanism between windows.

---

### Early sessions: trying to build the whole app at once

Claude did not treat the clone as a sequence of small, mergeable steps. It tried to implement a large portion of the app in a single pass—described in the post as attempting to **one-shot** the app.

That work ran long enough that the context window filled **in the middle of an implementation**. The session ended with a feature **half-implemented and undocumented**. There was no reliable handoff artifact describing what had been started, what remained, or what was broken.

---

### Next session after a mid-feature cutoff

A later instance started with a fresh context (compaction did not always pass “perfectly clear instructions”). It had to **guess** what the previous session had done.

A large part of that session was spent trying to **get the basic app working again**, rather than adding the next piece of the clone. The post states this recovery cost was substantial and recurred when a session died mid-implementation.

---

### Later in the project: stopping after seeing existing progress

After some features existed, a later instance inspected the repo, saw that work had already been done, and **declared the job done**. The remaining clone was not finished; the agent treated partial progress as completion.

---

### How Claude checked its own work (when it did)

When it made code changes, Claude sometimes ran **unit tests** or **curl against a development server**. Those checks were not enough for it to notice that a feature still failed **end-to-end as a human user would use it**. It still treated the feature as complete.

The post later contrasts this with explicit browser-automation prompting (Puppeteer MCP, screenshots). That is presented as a later intervention, not as default behavior on the original high-level prompt.

---

### Outcome of the unharnessed loop

Out of the box, even Opus 4.5 on the Claude Agent SDK, looped across windows with compaction, **did not produce a production-quality claude.ai clone** from the high-level prompt. Recurring end states were:

- a half-built, undocumented feature and a following session spent recovering the app;
- a later session that stopped because some features already existed;
- features marked done after code-level or curl checks even when they did not work end-to-end.

---

### After Anthropic added a two-part harness (same model, different prompts)

The post then describes a **changed** setup, not a separate mystery model: an **initializer** on the first window and a **coding agent** on later windows. System prompt, tools, and harness were otherwise the same; only the initial user prompt differed.

**Initializer (session 1)** was asked to stand up:

- `init.sh` to run the development server;
- `claude-progress.txt` as a log of what agents had done;
- an initial **git** commit of added files;
- a structured **feature list** expanding the user prompt.

For the claude.ai clone, that list had **over 200** features, each written as an end-to-end behavior (example: a user can open a new chat, type a query, press enter, and see an AI response). Every feature started with `"passes": false`. Example JSON:

```json
{
  "category": "functional",
  "description": "New chat button creates a fresh conversation",
  "steps": [
    "Navigate to main interface",
    "Click the 'New Chat' button",
    "Verify a new conversation is created",
    "Check that chat area shows welcome state",
    "Verify conversation appears in sidebar"
  ],
  "passes": false
}
```

Coding agents were told to change **only** the `passes` field, with wording such as: it is unacceptable to remove or edit tests because that could lead to missing or buggy functionality. JSON was used after experiments showed the model was less likely to overwrite JSON than Markdown.

**Coding agent (later sessions)** was asked to work on **one feature at a time**, leave a mergeable “clean state,” commit with descriptive messages, and write progress summaries. Git was used to revert bad changes.

---

### A typical later session under that harness (tool sequence from the post)

The coding agent was prompted to: `pwd`; read git logs and progress files; read the feature list and pick the highest-priority unfinished feature; use `init.sh` to start the server; run a basic end-to-end test **before** implementing anything new.

Quoted assistant/tool sequence:

1. “I'll start by getting my bearings and understanding the current state of the project.”
2. `bash` — `pwd`
3. Read `claude-progress.txt`
4. Read `feature_list.json`
5. “Let me check the git log to see recent work.”
6. `bash` — `git log --oneline -20`
7. Look for `init.sh` and restart servers; start the development server.
8. “Excellent! Now let me navigate to the application and verify that some fundamental features are still working.”
9. Test basic functionality (for the clone: start the local server, use Puppeteer MCP to start a new chat, send a message, receive a response).
10. After verification: core chat, theme switching, conversation loading, and error handling were reported working.
11. Review `tests.json` for the next unimplemented item and start that feature.

If that smoke test failed, the agent was expected to fix the breakage first; implementing a new feature on a broken app would make it worse.

---

### Testing after they added browser tools

Once explicitly told to use **browser automation** and test as a human user, Claude mostly verified web features end-to-end. It took **screenshots via the Puppeteer MCP** while testing the clone and used them to find and fix bugs that were not obvious from the code.

Remaining observed limits:

- Claude’s **vision** and the **browser automation tools** still missed some bugs.
- Claude **could not see browser-native alert modals** through the Puppeteer MCP; features that depended on those modals **tended to stay buggier**.

---

### What the post claims as the end of the harnessed run

With initializer artifacts, one-feature-at-a-time prompting, git + `claude-progress.txt`, `init.sh`, and end-to-end browser tests, later sessions could reconstruct state without guessing and without spending the window restoring a broken app. The demo is described as optimized for full-stack web apps; the post does not give a numeric “clone complete / N of 200 passing” result, only that this harness let the model make incremental progress across many windows, with the modal/vision gaps still open.

---

Sources: [Effective harnesses for long-running agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents); companion quickstart referenced in that post: [anthropics/claude-quickstarts (autonomous-coding)](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-quickstarts/tree/main/autonomous-coding).
